doc.title: Buster Williams interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 6, 2002

title: Teaching at the New School and the loss of places to hear live jazz
summary: He describes students after school, the lost Birdland and Jazz Gallery era, and says the music will survive like a roach.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Right. Very controversial. What’s replaced that thing for young musicians where they would stand on 52nd Street and follow their heroes?

There hasn’t been too much. There hasn’t been a replacement. In fact I teach at the New School. I’ve been there about six or seven years I guess. Maybe seven or eight years. And it’s very interesting to see what happens semester after semester. The great thing about the New School at first, and probably still is, was the fact that young musicians from all over the world could focus on coming to New York where the music thrives, where the music is born, where the music is being developed constantly. And study at a university with these musicians who are active and constantly re-developing the music. But where do they go after school? Nowadays you bring your students together and you find out that what they’re doing after school is this guy over here, he and his friend have a studio where they’ve got all of the latest Pro Tools and whatever, and they’re actively involved in becoming producers of new hip hoppers. And then this person over here is carrying on a day job or a part time job at a bakery or something and is looking for somewhere to go out and play his instrument. And this person here has his own band and he’s working at night at the Knitting Factory or these little unknown clubs. But none of them have anywhere to go where they can sit for an evening but just paying five dollars such as you used to be able to do at Birdland, the real Birdland, and sit there all evening and sip a glass of beer in the peanut gallery, and nobody bothered you. And you could listen to two bands — Miles Davis’ band and as soon as he finishes, here comes Sonny Rollins’ band. Or you go down to the Jazz Gallery and you listen and there is John Coltrane with his famous band with Elvin Jones and Jimmy Garrison. And when they get off the bandstand then there’s Horace Silver. Those kind of things don’t exist anymore. So what you try and do is make sure that all of your students have an opportunity to come hear your band, my band. Like next week I’m at the Vanguard. So all my students are going to come down to the Vanguard and they can hear the band. There was a little club for a while called Small’s. I don’t know if it still exists. But night after night all of the young guys and girls would crowd down there and hope to have a chance to play. There’s a few places around the city, but it’s not like it used to be. And now I’m not crying for it to be like it used to be. Nothing is like it used to be. That’s the nature of things. Everything changes. Everything is in a constant state of flux, as it should be. But there should be some wisdom that’s garnished, an accumulation of understanding how things go and how to make things better as we continue on. For something as alive as this music, it’s like a

proverbial roach you can never destroy it, I don’t care how many roaches you step on there’s always going to be millions coming afterwards. This music will always exist. But only because of its own nature. It would be great if there was some support of the music. If there was some kind of understanding of what it is that brought this music to us in the first place. And let’s be the perpetrators of those elements that allow the music to thrive and be the great cultural substance that it is. I mean you take it out of the culture — but who is advocating a day without music?
One day with no music anywhere. Quite different.
